1:
How old Joshua was cannot be fixed, and Gill says so, but reckons about a hundred, since Joshua lived to a hundred and ten, the Jews allow seven years for the dividing of Canaan, and he did not long survive it. Clarke gives the same figure and apportions the years: seven in the conquest, one in the division, ten before his death. Calvin denies that old and stricken in years is a tautology. The Jews used a threefold division of age, and the last stage, from the eightieth year to the end of life, is what the second phrase means; Joshua had reached it. Henry notes what that meant among the people he led: he and Caleb were by now the only old men in Israel, none of those numbered at Sinai being left alive but the two. Joshua had been a man of war from his youth, but was yielding to the infirmities of age, against which it is vain for the stoutest to contend; and Henry observes, comparing him with Moses, that he had not the same strength in age, for all who reach old age do not find it alike good.

That God should tell a man he is old is what Henry dwells on. It is good for those stricken in years to be put in mind of it, since some have grey hairs upon them and perceive it not, and do not care to think of it, and need telling, that they may be quickened to the work of life and prepared for a death coming on apace. Wesley keeps only that much. Henry then draws two reasons from the reminder. The first is that Joshua should lay aside the thought of pursuing the war. He could not expect to see the end of it, and it was not fit at his age to renew the fighting and carry it into distant parts; enough that he had reduced the body of the country. Let him be gathered to his rest with honour and the thanks of his people, and the conquering of the skirts left to those who came after, as he had entered into the labours of Moses; the top-stone was reserved for David long after. God considers the frame of his people, Henry adds, and will not have them burdened above their strength. The second reason is the opposite: what he could still do he must do quickly, and all people, old people especially, should set about what must be done before they die, lest death prevent them.

The unsubdued land raises the harder question, why divide what is not yet held. Keil and Delitzsch set the command at the head of the whole distribution, entered upon now that Joshua was old although parts of the country were still unconquered, with the account of the eastern territory appended. Clarke thinks Joshua had meant to subdue the whole land before dividing it, and that God did not allow it; the Israelites were so unfaithful that he seems to have purposed that some old inhabitants remain to keep them in check, each tribe having labour of its own in clearing its borders. Calvin allows that a pause after thirty-one kings had fallen was reasonable, provided they rested only for a time; but lest it become an occasion of sloth, the Lord applies a new spur, ordering even the enemy-held coast into the lot. Calvin knows how it looks: absurd and ludicrous, a complete mockery, that they should parcel out among themselves the property of others as if it were their own. The lot was to be an earnest of certain possession, keeping them in readiness; those whose portion fell in enemy country, living meanwhile as strangers on precarious hospitality, would act as taskmasters spurring the rest on. It had to be done while Joshua lived, no successor having authority enough for so difficult a task.
2:
Gill explains why the catalogue is given at all. It was for Joshua's information, that he might know what he had to divide, and for the people's, that they might know what they had a claim upon and what the Lord would deliver into their hands provided they were obedient; because they were not, many of these places never came into their possession, though divided to them by lot. Calvin reads the list as a recalling of the ancient boundaries fixed by God, so that Joshua and the people might be persuaded the covenant made with Abraham would be fulfilled in every part, and be enjoined to make it their study to acquire what remained. He turns it into a rule of perseverance, since Paul forgets what is behind and presses toward the mark, and it is no use running the race without endeavouring to reach the goal. Wesley states the condition flatly: the land remained unconquered, and was to be conquered by the Israelites if they behaved themselves aright.

The southern boundary is disputed. Gill reports that Jarchi and Kimchi take Sihor for the Nile, so called from its black and turbid waters, whence the Greek Melas and the Latin Melo; but he doubts the river itself is meant, since it did not reach the borders of Palestine, and cites a traveller on its nearest arm, five days from Gaza. Clarke prints a friend's opinion to the same effect: a wide desert lay between the river of Egypt and the isthmus of Suez, Solomon reigned to the borders of Egypt but not to the Nile, and black might be applied to another river. Keil and Delitzsch settle it: the Nile is always called simply the river in plain prose and was not before Egypt but flowed through the middle of it, so the Sichor here is the brook of Egypt. Calvin follows the received opinion for the Nile while refusing to repudiate the other. He then raises the question nobody else asks, why a sixth people, the Avites, follows five counted sea-coast territories. Some say they were left out as insignificant; Calvin asks his readers to consider an antithesis between a free people, their own masters, and five territories under sovereigns, and adds that the towns are listed by nearness to Egypt rather than by rank.

Clarke names the five lordships as Gaza, Ashdod, Askalon, Gath and Ekron, marks Ekron the most northern, and says there is no proof Israel ever possessed it, though it fell within the lot of Dan. He warns that the Avites are not the Hivites but an inconsiderable tribe already deprived of their country by the Caphtorim, and Wesley adds that though most were destroyed, many escaped and settled nearby; counted to the Canaanite means, on his reading, that land now held by Philistines is still part of Canaan and belongs to Israel. Northward the names give more trouble. Clarke reports Calmet's proposal to read Aramites for Amorites, since no Amorites are known in that quarter, an emendation of two letters that Houbigant approves though no version supports it. Gill and Keil agree in identifying the Giblites with Gebal, the Byblos of the Greeks, on the coast north of Beirut. On the promise to drive out the hill country and the Sidonians, Clarke insists the word was never unconditional, and meets the charge that Scripture failed by distinguishing what was promised: Joshua was to bring them in and divide the land, which he did, not to conquer the whole first. Calvin draws the positive lesson, that Joshua must not defer the partition for want of possession, since doubt of the event would detract from God's honour. Wesley keeps both halves: God will do his work in his own time, yet driving out before the children of Israel supposes they must go up against them.
7:
Henry catches the exchange behind the command. Joshua thought all must be conquered before any could be divided; God answers that enough is conquered to serve their turn, and that he should divide this and wait for the rest — from which Henry takes it that we must have the comfort of what we have, though we cannot compass all we would. Gill notes only that with God's authority for it Joshua was to begin at once. Henry then draws three things from the order. The land must be divided at all, and the tribes not always live in common; it is the will of the God who gave the earth to men that every man should know his own and not invade another's, and the world be governed by equity, not arms. It must be an inheritance, though won by conquest, since the promise came from their fathers and was to pass to their children; what is got by force is soon lost, but a title by divine grant is secured to the seed. And it must go by lot rather than by Joshua's will, wise and just as he was, the lot referring the matter wholly to God, who appoints the bounds of our habitation, though Joshua must preside and settle disputes. In dividing what he conquered, Henry adds, he was a type of Christ, who has opened the gates of heaven and will in due time put believers in possession.

Henry finds three reasons why the eastern grant is recited. It explains why only nine tribes and a half are provided for here. It gives Joshua a pattern, since he had watched Moses distribute that land. And it is a spur to hasten, so these tribes should not be kept from their possession while their brethren were settled, God their common Father not wishing such a difference among his children. Clarke states plainly that the two tribes and the other half of Manasseh had their portion in the land of Og and Sihon, and Gill adds that Reuben and Gad had asked for theirs, so had no share in this division. On the repeated words, which Moses gave them, even as Moses gave them, Henry sees a ratification: Moses settled it, and as he settled it, so shall it rest. Wesley turns them into an instruction, that Joshua is not to disturb those possessions but to divide the rest.

The boundaries begin at Aroer, which Gill calls a Moabite city on the Arnon, the border between Moab and the Amorites; Wesley traces Medeba and Dibon from Moab to the Amorites to Israel, and back to their first owners once Israel went into captivity. Keil and Delitzsch take Gilead for the whole country of that name on both sides of the Jabbok, and mark the awkwardness that follows: the Geshurite and Maachathite territory is counted into the inheritance, yet was never possessed, and had probably never been subject to Og at all. Gill records the failure without comment, that Israel expelled neither people under Moses or Joshua, and Wesley observes that God had given their land away though the gift went unused. The other exception is Levi. Keil explains that the tribe received no land but the firings of Jehovah, the offerings with tithes and firstfruits, so that God himself is called Levi's inheritance, and Gill says neither the Lord nor Moses appointed them a portion on either side of Jordan. Calvin thinks the notice necessary, lest the Levites allege they were unjustly disinherited and raise commotions about their right; Moses is named as the author of the distinction, and an excellent compensation was given, for as God allures them by hire to the charge of sacred things, he binds the people to pay the oblations that maintain them. Wesley says the repetition guards them against the malice, envy and covetousness of their brethren.
15:
Calvin asks why so much detail was needed and gives two reasons. The first is gratitude, the divine goodness being recorded in public documents and kept constantly before the people's eyes. The second is peace: each was to enjoy his inheritance without quarrel, and Calvin knows how ingenious human cupidity is in devising pretexts for litigation, so that no man holds his right in safety unless a plain definition makes it impossible to question. The eastern country had been given without casting lots, and it was open to others to object that the just proportion had not been kept. So the boundaries are fixed by God's own authority. He does not merely adjudge the kingdom of Sihon to Reuben but traces the limit from Aroer along the Arnon and round the whole circuit, leaving not a single acre ambiguous. The care God took to cherish peace shows a truly paternal love; had it not been taken thus early they might have been consumed by quarrels among themselves. Calvin then begs to be excused from labouring over the situation of the towns. Wesley notes that the division by families holds of the greater families only, lesser allotments being left to inferior officers under rules Moses had given.

Keil and Delitzsch supply what Calvin declined. Reuben's portion lay in the south, from Aroer in the Arnon valley across the table-land by Medeba, with Heshbon its capital. Heshbon stood midway between the Arnon and the Jabbok, on the border of the inheritance, and was ceded to Gad, who gave it to the Levites; Dibon is called Dibon of Gad because the Gadites fortified it; Bamoth-baal is to be sought on the Jebel Attarus, from which Balaam looked out; and Sibmah, which Jerome puts five hundred paces from Heshbon, has hopelessly disappeared. Clarke places Kirjathaim nine miles east of Medeba on Eusebius's authority and traces its owners from the Emim through the Moabites and Amorites to Israel, adding from Calmet that Moab took it back when Reuben went into captivity. On the phrase in the mount of the valley he and Wesley are cautious, Clarke supposing a town on a hill in flat country, Wesley the mountain bordering a valley then famous in Israel, and thinking the clause belongs to all the cities named. Gill explains Beth-peor from Peor, the Moabite idol, where a temple to it had likely stood.

The naming of the Midianite princes as dukes of Sihon is what Ellicott seizes. Numbers gives one reason for that war, Midian's tempting Israel to idolatry; this verse supplies another, that the Midianites were part of Sihon's government, through whom he held the territory taken from Moab, so that removing his dukes was needed to complete the conquest. The relation between Midian and Moab is implied in Numbers but never explained there, and Ellicott calls the casual remark here another undesigned agreement between Joshua and the Pentateuch. He reads the epithet given to Balaam the same way: Numbers reports only prophecy and counsel from his lips, yet the elders came with the reward of divination in their hands, and the word used here shows a man who, failing to get the knowledge he wanted from above, would seek it below for base gain. Clarke takes the opposite view, that both verses seem borrowed from Numbers and that Balaam's death is quite irrelevant here. Calvin finds it pointed: the princes are called satraps to show they fell in the same overthrow, having joined an unjust war, and Balaam is named among the slain because his tongue had tried to wound Israel worse than a thousand swords. Gill passes on Kimchi's guess that Balaam went back to Midian for his wages once his counsel took effect, and the Jewish account that Phinehas killed him. Wesley says the notice is repeated because the turning of that curse into a blessing deserved everlasting remembrance.
24:
Keil and Delitzsch set out Gad's territory: Jazer and all the towns of Gilead, meaning the southern half that had been Sihon's, the northern half having been Og's and going to Manasseh; northward the boundary seems to have run to the Jabbok, passing beyond it only at Mahanaim, while in the Jordan valley it reached the Sea of Galilee. The phrase half the land of the children of Ammon needs explaining, and three of the writers explain it the same way. Keil takes it for the strip between the Arnon and the Jabbok that Sihon's Amorites had taken from Ammon, the land Ammon still held further east being what Israel was forbidden to attack. Clarke states the principle: Israel might not take Ammonite land, but this portion, annexed to Sihon's kingdom, came to them by conquest when they defeated him. Wesley says the same, that the land meant is not what was then Ammon's but what had anciently been theirs until the Amorites took it. On the cities of Gilead Wesley adds that only cities of eminence are meant, which squares with the later verse where half of Gilead goes to Manasseh with no cities named; Aroer he makes the border toward Moab, Rabbah the chief Ammonite city. Gill notes that Jazer, their southern limit here, is spoken of as a city of Moab by the later prophets.

The names along the border draw short notes. Gill identifies Ramath-mizpeh with Ramoth-gilead, which Jerome knew as a village two miles from Rabbath, and confesses that Betonim is nowhere else mentioned, so can only place it near Ramath. Clarke agrees, and adds that it was a city of refuge. On Mahanaim he gives the meaning, the two camps, sets it north of the brook Jabbok, and recalls the vision of the two camps of angels Jacob saw there; Wesley reads the boundary as excluding the town itself, since Mahanaim lay in Manasseh's portion beyond the Jabbok, which divided Gad from Manasseh. Clarke has the fullest note on Beth-aram, which Herod rebuilt and named Livias after the wife of Augustus, though Josephus calls it Julias, the name the Greeks commonly gave her; and he derives Succoth, between Jabbok and Jordan, from Jacob's pitching his tents there.

Why half of Manasseh should be settled east of the river at all is Clarke's question, since when Reuben and Gad asked for that side no part of Manasseh appears to have joined them; his answer is that the tribe was numerous and had much cattle, so Moses appointed one half to stay and the other to cross. Wesley offers two further motives, a recompense to Machir for his valiant acts against Og, and the better defence of the other two tribes by so considerable an accession, which cost them nothing since the country was too large for Reuben and Gad alone. Gill leaves it open whether the grant was asked for or made unprompted. Keil runs the territory from Mahanaim over all Bashan with the sixty towns of Jair and the northern half of Gilead, and marks the last two verses as the closing formula and a repetition of the earlier notice on Levi. Calvin ends on the two things the list is for. God is extolled for his liberality in expelling nations of great celebrity and putting Israel in their room, which the counting of sixty cities makes plain, so that nobody may think Moses munificent by mistake; and the exclusion of Levi is repeated in a short clause lest the Levites should afterwards pretend that a grant made without casting lots belonged to them in common. Here, Calvin observes, it is not the sacrifices but God himself who is called their inheritance, and if they are not satisfied with that they convict themselves of insufferable pride.
